title: Metre and scansion: hearing iambic pentameter and how poets bend it
examples: How do you scan a line of poetry?

explain.say: Put your hand on your chest. Your heartbeat goes da-DUM, da-DUM, soft then strong. That pattern, an iamb, is the basic beat of English verse. Five of them make a line of iambic pentameter: penta is Greek for five, and metre means measure. Shakespeare, Milton and Wordsworth wrote much of their verse in it.

explain.say: A foot is one unit of beats. Sort the words on the board. An iamb is soft then strong, like today. A trochee is strong then soft, like garden. An anapest is soft, soft, strong, like understand, and a dactyl is strong, soft, soft, like elephant. Say each word aloud and tap the strong syllable. Which foot is your own name?

Now scan a line step by step, following the chain. Take Shakespeare's line: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day. Count ten syllables. Mark the strong beats by saying it naturally. Divide it into five pairs, each soft then strong. Name it: iambic pentameter. Then look for where the pattern breaks. Try it with me now.

explain.say: Great poets bend the beat. Hamlet's line, To be, or not to be, that is the question, has eleven syllables, with an extra soft one at the end, called a feminine ending, which leaves the line hanging, like Hamlet himself. Lines often start with a trochee for a punch, or pause in the middle, a caesura. Why give a hesitating prince a hesitating line?

The same beat wears different outfits. Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter, used by Marlowe, Shakespeare and Milton. Heroic couplets rhyme in pairs, as in Pope. The English sonnet packs fourteen of these lines with a rhyme scheme. Brilliant. Challenge: write one line of perfect iambic pentameter about your breakfast, then start it with a trochee instead.

faq.a: A line of verse with five iambs, each a soft syllable followed by a strong one, making ten syllables in a da-DUM rhythm. It is the most common metre in English poetry.

faq.q: How do you scan a line of poetry?
faq.a: Count the syllables, mark which are stressed by saying the line naturally, divide the line into feet, name the foot and the number of feet, then note any variations and what they emphasise.
A metrical foot of one strong syllable followed by a soft one, like garden or tyger. Poets often put a trochee at the start of an iambic line for emphasis.
Unrhymed iambic pentameter. Marlowe made it the voice of the Elizabethan stage, Shakespeare used it for most of his verse, and Milton wrote Paradise Lost in it.
An extra unstressed syllable at the end of a line of verse, making eleven syllables in pentameter. It can make a line sound softer, unresolved or hesitant.

facts: Blank verse first appeared in English in the Earl of Surrey's translation of Virgil in the 1540s.
Christopher Marlowe made blank verse the standard voice of the stage with Tamburlaine around 1587.
Paradise Lost has more than ten thousand lines of blank verse.
